title: Who Turns the Tap
endLine: Arterioles are every organ's tap; organs differ in who turns it.

scenes.tts: With mean arterial pressure held steady, each tissue sets its own flow by its arterioles. But who turns that tap? And what does it listen to?
scenes.narration: With mean arterial pressure held steady, each tissue sets its own flow by its arterioles. But who turns that tap? And what does it listen to?
scenes.caption: With mean arterial pressure held steady, each tissue sets its own flow by its arterioles. But who turns that tap? And what does it listen to?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's world and colour map without a reset: blood pale RED dots; pressure WHITE; arterioles and their smooth-muscle rings ORANGE (the tap), each with a small tap-handle icon; capillaries CYAN; small artery, venule and vein SLATE; the muscle bed's flow GOLD. New in this film: signals from the tissue itself GREEN dots; nitric oxide from the vessel lining BLUE dots; nerves PURPLE wires. A small 'schematic' tag sits at bottom right all film. OPENING (recap, on the first sentence): the first film's loop, a SLATE aorta with its WHITE gauge tagged 'held nearly steady' feeding the muscle branch and the 'other beds' branch into the right atrium; the tap icons on both ORANGE arterioles glow once. Then the camera glides into the muscle branch and rearranges it into this film's main layout: LEFT 55% of the frame holds one bed filling about 70% of frame height: a WHITE 'perfusion pressure' gauge on the incoming SLATE artery, the ORANGE arteriole with its rings, then a pale block of tissue threaded with CYAN capillaries, then the outgoing vein with a GOLD 'flow' bar beside it. RIGHT 45% is kept empty for a plot (from s03). On 'who turns that tap', a large hand outline hovers over the arteriole's tap icon with a '?'. White text across the top: 'Who turns the tap?'
Title 'Who Turns the Tap' fades in above the bed for 2 s while the question text fades out. Red dots keep flowing through the arteriole and capillaries; the ORANGE rings breathe gently.

scenes.tts: When a tissue works harder, its arterioles relax and flow follows. No single signal does it; several overlap. From the working tissue come adenosine, potassium, carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and low oxygen. The vessel lining, the endothelium, adds nitric oxide.
scenes.narration: When a tissue works harder, its arterioles relax and flow follows. No single signal does it; several overlap. From the working tissue come adenosine, K+, CO2, H+ and low O2. The vessel lining, the endothelium, adds nitric oxide.
scenes.caption: When a tissue works harder, its arterioles relax and flow follows. No single signal does it; several overlap. From the working tissue come adenosine, K+, CO2, H+ and low O2. The vessel lining, the endothelium, adds nitric oxide.
scenes.visual: The tissue block brightens and pulses faster, tagged 'working'. GREEN dots seep out of it toward the arteriole, tagged 'tissue signals'; as the list is spoken, short GREEN tags appear one at a time beside the stream and stack into a column: 'adenosine', 'K⁺', 'CO₂', 'H⁺', 'low O₂' (they replace the 'working' tag, so no more than six things show). On 'endothelium', the inner lining of the arteriole glows and releases BLUE dots into its wall, tagged 'nitric oxide'. The ORANGE rings relax, the arteriole widens, red dots speed up, and the GOLD flow bar rises. On 'several overlap', the GREEN and BLUE streams interleave at the wall.

scenes.tts: The same tap does a second job. It can hold flow steady when perfusion pressure changes, while the tissue's demand stays the same. This is autoregulation.
scenes.narration: The same tap does a second job. It can hold flow steady when perfusion pressure changes, while the tissue's demand stays the same. This is autoregulation.
scenes.caption: The same tap does a second job. It can hold flow steady when perfusion pressure changes, while the tissue's demand stays the same. This is autoregulation.
scenes.visual: The GREEN and BLUE tags fade; the tissue block calms to a steady glow tagged 'demand fixed'. The arteriole returns to its resting width. The WHITE 'perfusion pressure' gauge starts to slide slowly up, then down, then up again; the GOLD flow bar barely moves. On 'autoregulation', the word appears large above the bed, size 34. On the right, empty axes fade in: x axis 'perfusion pressure', y axis 'flow', no numbers, tag 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Plot pressure along the bottom, flow up the side. At low pressures, flow rises with pressure. Across a middle range, the line runs nearly level, though not perfectly flat. Above that range, flow rises again.
scenes.narration: Plot pressure along the bottom, flow up the side. At low pressures, flow rises with pressure. Across a middle range, the line runs nearly level, though not perfectly flat. Above that range, flow rises again.
scenes.caption: Plot pressure along the bottom, flow up the side. At low pressures, flow rises with pressure. Across a middle range, the line runs nearly level, though not perfectly flat. Above that range, flow rises again.
scenes.visual: A WHITE dot, driven by the gauge on the left, draws a schematic curve on the right plot as the gauge sweeps from low to high: a rising stretch at low pressures; a long middle stretch that is nearly level but tilts slightly upward (visibly not flat); and a rising stretch again at high pressures. On 'middle range', that stretch is bracketed with the label 'nearly level'. The 'schematic' tag stays. The low end gets no label or explanation. The gauge then returns to the middle of the range and the dot sits on the nearly level stretch.

scenes.tts: Remember: flow equals pressure drop divided by resistance. Across that middle range, pressure climbs but flow barely moves. So what must the arterioles be doing?
scenes.narration: Remember: flow equals pressure drop divided by resistance. Across that middle range, pressure climbs but flow barely moves. So what must the arterioles be doing?
scenes.caption: Remember: flow equals pressure drop divided by resistance. Across that middle range, pressure climbs but flow barely moves. So what must the arterioles be doing?
scenes.visual: The first film's equation returns above the bed, size 34: 'flow = pressure drop ÷ resistance'. The WHITE gauge climbs slowly within the middle range; the dot on the plot slides along the nearly level stretch; the GOLD flow bar stays almost still. The ORANGE arteriole is outlined with a '?' beside it, its width not yet changing. Question text at the top in white: 'What are the arterioles doing?'

Predict pause. The question card stays. Near-stillness by design: the gauge hovers in the middle range, the plot dot bobs on the nearly level stretch, red dots drift slowly, and the '?' beside the arteriole pulses faintly.

scenes.tts: Narrowing. For flow to stay put while pressure rises, resistance must rise in proportion. When pressure falls, they widen. One mechanism is the myogenic response: a small artery reacting to the pressure across its wall.
scenes.narration: Narrowing. For flow to stay put while pressure rises, resistance must rise in proportion. When pressure falls, they widen. One mechanism is the myogenic response: a small artery reacting to the pressure across its wall.
scenes.caption: Narrowing. For flow to stay put while pressure rises, resistance must rise in proportion. When pressure falls, they widen. One mechanism is the myogenic response: a small artery reacting to the pressure across its wall.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. As the WHITE gauge climbs within the middle range, the ORANGE rings tighten and the arteriole narrows; a WHITE 'resistance' bar beside it rises in proportion with the gauge, while the GOLD flow bar stays nearly level. On 'When pressure falls', the gauge eases down, the rings relax, the arteriole widens and the resistance bar falls, flow still nearly level. On 'myogenic response', small outward arrows press on the arteriole wall from inside, and the rings answer by tightening; label 'myogenic response'. The plot dot stays on the nearly level stretch throughout.

scenes.tts: In the heart, flow tracks oxygen use. In nineteen sixty-three, Robert Berne made cat and dog hearts short of oxygen. Coronary resistance fell, and the muscle released breakdown products of adenosine.
scenes.narration: In the heart, flow tracks oxygen use. In 1963, Robert Berne made cat and dog hearts short of oxygen. Coronary resistance fell, and the muscle released breakdown products of adenosine.
scenes.caption: In the heart, flow tracks oxygen use. In 1963, Robert Berne made cat and dog hearts short of oxygen. Coronary resistance fell, and the muscle released breakdown products of adenosine.
scenes.visual: The plot on the right fades out. The tissue block morphs into a block of heart muscle with faint striations, relabelled 'heart muscle'; the arteriole is now labelled 'coronary arteriole'. A small tag 'Berne, 1963' appears at top left. On 'short of oxygen', a small CYAN-outlined oxygen gauge beside the block drains (schematic). On 'resistance fell', the ORANGE rings relax, the arteriole widens and the WHITE resistance bar drops. On 'breakdown products', GREEN dots leave the muscle into the vein, labelled 'breakdown products' (no molecular drawings).

scenes.tts: He proposed that adenosine forms as A T P breaks down when oxygen supply falls short. It diffuses to the arterioles and dilates them. Later blockade studies in dogs found it a potent dilator. But its role is not evident unless oxygen delivery is compromised.
scenes.narration: He proposed that adenosine forms as ATP breaks down when oxygen supply falls short. It diffuses to the arterioles and dilates them. Later blockade studies in dogs found it a potent dilator. But its role is not evident unless oxygen delivery is compromised.
scenes.caption: He proposed that adenosine forms as ATP breaks down when oxygen supply falls short. It diffuses to the arterioles and dilates them. Later blockade studies in dogs found it a potent dilator. But its role is not evident unless oxygen delivery is compromised.
scenes.visual: Inside the heart block, a GREEN token labelled 'ATP' splits into a smaller GREEN token labelled 'adenosine', with a tag 'Berne's proposal'. The adenosine token drifts to the ORANGE arteriole; the rings relax and the arteriole widens. On 'blockade studies', a plain bar labelled 'blocker' slides across the adenosine path. Two small side-by-side flow bars appear beside the heart, labelled 'normal oxygen' and 'oxygen short' (schematic): under the blocker the 'normal oxygen' bar barely changes, while the 'oxygen short' bar falls short of its outline. A tag 'other signals likely overlap' sits under them.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. In every organ, the arterioles are the tap. What changes from organ to organ is who turns it.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. In every organ, the arterioles are the tap. What changes from organ to organ is who turns it.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. In every organ, the arterioles are the tap. What changes from organ to organ is who turns it.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back to the first film's parallel world, now with four branches off the SLATE aorta, all rejoining at the right atrium and together filling about 70% of frame height: 'heart', 'brain', 'muscle' (GOLD-tinted dots) and 'skin'. Each branch has the same ORANGE arteriole with its tap-handle icon. On 'the arterioles are the tap', all four tap icons glow together. On 'who turns it', a different empty hand outline appears over each tap. Text across the top, size 34: 'Same tap. Different hands.' The WHITE aorta gauge stays steady.

scenes.tts: In the heart, metabolism turns it. In the brain, active neurons raise local flow. Carbon dioxide matters too: a rise dilates brain vessels, and a fall constricts them.
scenes.narration: In the heart, metabolism turns it. In the brain, active neurons raise local flow. Carbon dioxide matters too: a rise dilates brain vessels, and a fall constricts them.
scenes.caption: In the heart, metabolism turns it. In the brain, active neurons raise local flow. Carbon dioxide matters too: a rise dilates brain vessels, and a fall constricts them.
scenes.visual: The heart branch brightens: GREEN tissue-signal dots fill its hand outline and its tap turns; tag 'metabolism'. Then the brain branch brightens: a small neuron icon beside it sparks and its arteriole widens, tag 'neural activity'. A small gauge beside the brain labelled 'CO₂' rises and the brain arteriole widens; it falls and the arteriole narrows. The other branches stay dim but flowing.

scenes.tts: In working muscle, metabolites turn it. In human studies, no single dilator explains much more than twenty to thirty percent of the rise. Working muscle also blunts sympathetic constriction.
scenes.narration: In working muscle, metabolites turn it. In human studies, no single dilator explains much more than 20 to 30 percent of the rise. Working muscle also blunts sympathetic constriction.
scenes.caption: In working muscle, metabolites turn it. In human studies, no single dilator explains much more than 20 to 30 percent of the rise. Working muscle also blunts sympathetic constriction.
scenes.visual: The muscle branch brightens: GREEN metabolite dots fill its hand outline, its arteriole widens and GOLD dots stream faster. Beside it a single bar labelled 'flow rise' splits into several stacked slices of different colours, none bigger than about a quarter of the bar, tag 'no single dilator'. On 'sympathetic nerves', a PURPLE nerve wire running to the muscle arteriole keeps pulsing to tighten the rings, but the rings barely tighten as the muscle keeps working; tag 'constriction blunted'.

scenes.tts: In skin, nerves turn it. Skin flow follows body temperature more than the skin's own metabolism. In human whole-body heating, it has been estimated to reach six to eight liters a minute.
scenes.narration: In skin, nerves turn it. Skin flow follows body temperature more than the skin's own metabolism. In human whole-body heating, it has been estimated to reach 6 to 8 L per min.
scenes.caption: In skin, nerves turn it. Skin flow follows body temperature more than the skin's own metabolism. In human whole-body heating, it has been estimated to reach 6 to 8 L per min.
scenes.visual: The skin branch brightens. PURPLE nerve wires reach its arteriole and fill its hand outline. A thermometer icon labelled 'body temperature' rises; as it does, the nerves pulse, the skin arteriole widens and red dots pour through the skin branch. A small tag beside the skin branch: 'heating: estimated 6–8 L/min'. The skin tissue itself stays at a steady, dim glow (its own metabolism not the driver).

scenes.tts: The tap is the same everywhere. The hand on it is not: pressure, the tissue's own chemistry, neurons, or nerves tuned to body heat.
scenes.narration: The tap is the same everywhere. The hand on it is not: pressure, the tissue's own chemistry, neurons, or nerves tuned to body heat.
scenes.caption: The tap is the same everywhere. The hand on it is not: pressure, the tissue's own chemistry, neurons, or nerves tuned to body heat.
scenes.visual: All four branches brighten together, each tap turning with its own hand: on 'pressure', a small wall-stretch arrow on each arteriole (the myogenic response, as in s07); on 'own chemistry', GREEN dots at heart and muscle; on 'neurons', the spark at the brain; on 'nerves tuned to body heat', the PURPLE wires and thermometer at the skin. The WHITE aorta gauge stays steady; red dots flow through all four branches.

End card over the dimmed but still moving four-branch world (red dots flowing, ORANGE rings breathing gently). Large white text, centred: 'Arterioles are every organ's tap; organs differ in who turns it.'
